strengths: Provides a complete, self-contained diagrammatic (Feynman) framework for computing finite-width $1/n$ corrections to NTK statistics and joint preactivation–NTK statistics, extending prior diagrammatic work that was restricted to preactivation statistics only.

Theoretical claims are backed by explicit proofs: Theorem 4.1–4.3 establish that the rules recover the known NTK recursion relations and generalize to all orders, and Theorem 5.1 extends criticality/stability from preactivations to all NTK cumulants.

Delivers concrete new results, notably the layer-wise recursion for the first-order correction to the NTK mean and the proof (Theorem 5.2) that $\Theta(x,x)$ receives no finite-width corrections for scale-invariant nonlinearities, extending a known ReLU result to general scale-invariant activations.

First numerical implementation of the full coupled recursion relations in the general multi-input case, with Monte-Carlo verification showing corrected kernels track sampled GeLU/ReLU networks already at widths $n\gtrsim 20$ (Figures 1, 4–10, 22–25).

Limitations are discussed honestly (restriction to MLPs, mostly order $1/n$), and reproducibility is supported by detailed appendices on the SymPy/JAX implementation, integration settings, sample sizes, and compute resources.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate and incremental: the diagrammatic/QFT program for neural-network statistics is pre-existing, and the paper itself repeatedly notes that many derived recursions (for $D$, $F$, $A$, $B$, $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$, $T$, $U$) 'agree with the expression found in [17] using algebraic manipulations,' so much of the technical content is re-derivation rather than new results.

The practical payoff of the framework is not clearly demonstrated. The motivation is understanding training dynamics/feature learning, but the paper only studies initialization statistics; how the computed corrections would be used to predict or improve training is left unaddressed, and the recursions require expensive high-dimensional numerical integrals.

Empirical scope is limited: experiments use shallow (four-layer) MLPs and modest widths, and the 'all-order' theorems (5.1, 5.2) are largely supported by sampling at order $1/n$; higher-order claims are only spot-checked (one $1/n^2$ example in Appendix F).

The core rules depend heavily on dense, hard-to-parse diagrams and numerous appendices (C, D, E), making the main text difficult to follow and the correctness of the rules hard to verify independently from the presented material.

The central claim of exactness of the recursion relations and the new $\Theta^{\{1\}}$ recursion is verified mainly at a single depth (layer four); broader validation across depths, activations, and input scales would strengthen confidence.

strengths: Introduces a systematic diagrammatic (Feynman-style) calculus for finite-width corrections to NTK statistics, extending prior diagrammatic work on preactivation statistics to kernels that involve the NTK, dNTK and ddNTK.

The framework is internally consistent: the authors verify that their rules reproduce essentially all known recursion relations for V, D, F, A, B and the higher-derivative tensors P, Q, R, S, T, U from [17], which is a useful correctness check.
Derives a recursion relation for the first-order NTK-mean correction Theta^{1}, which the authors claim (plausibly) had not been obtained before.

Extends criticality/stability results from preactivations to NTK statistics (Theorem 5.1) and generalizes the absence of finite-width corrections for the NTK diagonal beyond the known ReLU case to general scale-invariant nonlinearities (Theorem 5.2).

Provides a fairly complete numerical implementation (SymPy symbolic recursions with custom Gaussian-expectation handling, numerical integration, JAX/neural-tangents Monte-Carlo) and verifies the first-order corrections for many tensors at widths n >= ~20.
Includes an honest limitations section acknowledging the restriction to MLPs and mostly to order 1/n.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the diagrammatic machinery is largely imported from the physics literature (e.g. [18, 26, 28, 29, 32, 33]), and its extension to NTK statistics, while non-trivial, is a fairly mechanical application of the same diagrammatic expansion rather than a new conceptual method.

The Feynman rules are 'postulated' and then validated by showing that they reproduce the known recursions of [17] (Theorems 4.1-4.3). This is a consistency check, not an independent derivation; the claims of 'uniqueness' and 'completeness at all orders' are argued heuristically rather than rigorously established.

The genuinely new results are modest in scope: a single additional recursion for Theta^{1}; a generalization of the ReLU scale-invariance result [38, 39] to general scale-invariant functions; and a confirmatory extension of known criticality results to NTK statistics.

The experiments primarily confirm the 1/n expansion (corrected kernels matching sampled networks), which is expected behavior for a first-order truncation; they do not yield new ML insights about training, feature learning, or architecture design.

The central selling point—'dramatically simplifying the algebraic manipulations'—is asserted but not convincingly demonstrated. The resulting rules involve ten tensors, many vertices and intricate selection rules, and one could argue the diagrams are themselves as complex as the algebra they replace.

Presentation is dense and physics-heavy, with a large fraction of the essential rules, vertices, and derivations deferred to appendices and appearing garbled in the provided manuscript, making the framework hard for an ML audience to follow or reproduce.
Scope is restricted to MLPs and (except for the stability analysis) to leading order in 1/n, so the generality implied by the abstract is not fully realized in the results.

strengths: Introduces a Feynman-diagram formalism for finite-width corrections to NTK statistics, extending previous preactivation-only diagrammatic methods to NTK, dNTK, and ddNTK tensors. The rules are summarized and Theorems 4.1-4.3 argue that they recover the known 1/n recursions and extend to all orders.

Derives a new layer-wise recursion for the first-order correction to the NTK mean (Section 5.1) and uses the formalism to prove that if the NNGP is critical then all cumulants involving the NTK are critical (Theorem 5.1), and that the diagonal NTK mean receives no finite-width corrections for scale-invariant activations (Theorem 5.2).

Implements the complete set of first-order recursions for the general multi-input case, including the NNGP, NTK, V, A, B, D, F tensors, and validates them against Monte-Carlo estimates from GeLU MLPs, with agreement already at widths n > 20 (Figures 1, 4-10).

Provides additional numerical verification of the stability analysis for ReLU MLPs, showing linear scaling of NTK statistics at criticality and exponential behavior away from it (Figure 2 and Appendix K), and confirms the predicted activation-function dependence of kernel corrections for ReLU, LeakyReLU, identity, and GeLU (Figures 3, 22-25).
The paper is candid about limitations, clearly stating the restriction to MLPs and mostly to order 1/n, and it points to possible extensions.
weaknesses: The demonstrated architecture is a bias-free MLP (Appendix B, eq. 17); biases and other common architectural components are not incorporated or discussed in detail, which limits the immediate generality of the framework and experiments.

The numerical evaluation is mostly restricted to first-order corrections at a single depth (four layers) and a few inputs/activation functions; higher-order all-order claims (Theorem 4.3) are not empirically stress-tested beyond a brief 1/n^2 consistency check (Appendix F).

Despite the motivation of predicting training dynamics and feature learning, the experiments focus on kernel statistics at initialization rather than demonstrating an end-to-end training-dynamics prediction. The practical ML payoff is therefore not fully demonstrated.

The main-text presentation is dense and relies heavily on appendices; many Feynman rules are given as diagrams whose full definitions are deferred, making the framework less accessible to the broader ICML audience.

No code or symbolic implementation is released, even though the numerical implementation of the recursions is a significant part of the contribution. Reproducing the full set of equations and the custom SymPy/NumPy/SciPy pipeline would require substantial reimplementation effort.

The proofs of the all-order statements (especially Theorem 4.3 and parts of Theorem 5.1) are somewhat diagrammatic and heuristic, relying on uniqueness/selection-rule arguments rather than a fully formal inductive proof; the claims are plausible but not airtight for a reader seeking rigorous guarantees.

The comparison to prior finite-width correction methods is mostly qualitative (agreement with known recursions), and the paper does not provide a systematic quantitative benchmark against alternative finite-width approaches beyond the sampling experiments.
